content:
Arthritis can shrink your world: pain, tiredness and worry about falling make it harder to get out, and seeing fewer people can then make pain and low mood feel worse. Start small and plan around your joints, such as one phone call a day, a short visit at the time you are least stiff, or a group with seating and easy access. Free phone friendship services, befriending schemes and your GP surgery's social prescribing link worker can help. If loneliness has turned into low mood for more than two weeks, talk to your GP or refer yourself to NHS talking therapies. If you feel you cannot go on, call Samaritans on 116 123 or 999 in an emergency.

This guide is for people with arthritis who are seeing fewer people than they would like, and for the family, friends and neighbours who worry about them. If low mood is the bigger problem, see depression and arthritis: when to get help. If you have recently lost a partner, see living alone after a bereavement.

How arthritis and loneliness feed each other

Many people with arthritis find their social life gets smaller without ever deciding it should. It often happens step by step:

  • Pain and stiffness make buses, steps, long walks and hard chairs difficult, so you say no to things.
  • Tiredness means you save your energy for essentials, and seeing people falls off the list.
  • Worry about falling, needing the toilet or not being able to get up from a low seat makes going out feel risky.
  • You stop driving or a partner who drove dies, and getting anywhere becomes harder.
  • Hearing or eyesight problems make conversation tiring, especially in noisy places.

Being alone a lot can then make pain feel harder to cope with and mood lower. The NHS lists illness and disability, living alone and bereavement among common causes of loneliness. It is not a personal failing, and it can be changed.

Start small and plan around your joints

The NHS advises not trying to do everything at once and setting small targets you can achieve. Some ideas:

  • One contact a day. A phone call, a video call or a chat over the garden fence all count.
  • Pick your best time. If you are stiff in the morning, invite people round in the afternoon. Use the energy you have for the people who matter to you; see pacing and energy management.
  • Invite people to you. A short visit at home is often easier than going out. It is fine to say you can manage an hour.
  • Check the venue first. Ring ahead to ask about parking, steps, toilets and chairs with arms. Choose cafés and groups where you know you can sit comfortably.
  • Put something in the diary. Having a regular thing to look forward to each week helps.
  • Talk to people you already see, such as at the pharmacy, the shop or the GP waiting room.

Help that comes to you

  • The Silver Line Helpline, run by Age UK, is a free phone line for people aged 55 and over, open 24 hours a day, every day, on 0800 4 70 80 90. You can call just to chat.
  • Telephone and face-to-face befriending. Age UK's telephone friendship service and local befriending schemes match you with a volunteer who calls or visits regularly. The Royal Voluntary Service and other local charities run similar schemes.
  • Video calls with family. If your hands make a phone fiddly, a tablet on a stand, voice control or larger buttons may help. Ask a family member or a local digital help session to set it up.

Getting out with less strain

  • Social prescribing. Ask your GP surgery about a social prescribing link worker. They can help you find local groups and activities that suit your mobility. See social prescribing.
  • Groups built around gentle movement, such as slow walking groups, seated exercise classes or swimming sessions, give you company and help your joints.
  • Faith and community groups, lunch clubs and day centres. See faith groups and access.
  • Transport. Community transport schemes run door-to-door minibuses and volunteer drivers for people who cannot use buses easily.
  • Volunteering from home or in a seated role can bring regular contact and a sense of purpose.
  • Online groups for people with arthritis can help with the feeling that nobody understands, though they work best alongside real-life contact.

Deal with what is keeping you in

  • Pain. If pain stops you going out, ask your GP or pharmacist for a review of your pain treatment. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.
  • Fear of falling. A physiotherapist can help with strength and balance, and the right walking aid can make outings safer. See rebuilding confidence after a fall.
  • Hearing and sight. Get your hearing and eyes checked if conversations have become hard work.
  • Help at home. If daily tasks leave no energy for anything else, ask your council for a needs assessment.

When loneliness becomes low mood

Feeling lonely is not the same as depression, but one can lead to the other. NICE guidance on long-term pain recognises the effect pain can have on mood and daily life. The NHS advises seeing a GP if you have had a low mood for more than two weeks or what you are trying is not helping. In England you can refer yourself to NHS talking therapies without seeing a GP.

  • If you need help urgently but it is not an emergency, call NHS 111.
  • If you feel you cannot go on or might harm yourself, call Samaritans free on 116 123 at any time, or call 999 or go to A&E.

For family, friends and neighbours

  • Regular, short contact often means more than occasional long visits.
  • Offer specific help, such as a lift to a group or setting up a video call, rather than a general offer.
  • Notice changes such as not answering the phone, not eating or seeming low, and encourage a GP visit.
  • If you are a carer, look after your own contact with others too; see our guide to helping without taking over.

Common questions

Is it normal to feel lonely with arthritis?

Yes. Many people with long-term pain feel cut off at times. Talking about it is a good first step.

I do not want to join a group. What else is there?

One-to-one phone or home befriending, regular calls with family, or a single activity you enjoy can all help. Start with what feels manageable.

Can my GP help with loneliness?

Yes. Your GP surgery can refer you to a social prescribing link worker and can help if loneliness is affecting your mood or health.
